ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there are four circles with the same radius, and the gray region is inside the middle circle. On the left, upper right, and lower right, there is respectively an adjacent circle intersecting the middle circle, and the gray boundary is pieced together from these circular arcs. Reasoning: According to the specified method, regard the gray region as the remaining part after the middle circle of radius 1 is cut into by three adjacent unit circles. For any adjacent circle, let its two intersection points with the middle circle be A and B. The original arc AB on the circumference of the middle circle that was cut away is replaced on the boundary of the gray region by the corresponding arc AB on the adjacent circle. Because the two circles have the same radius and share the same chord AB, their corresponding central angles are the same, and the arc lengths are also the same. Therefore each “replacement” caused by an adjacent circle does not change the total perimeter. All three adjacent circles are like this, so the perimeter of the gray region is equal to the circumference of a circle of radius 1, namely 2π.

raw_record.question_text: Four circles with radius 1 intersect each other as seen in the diagram. What is the perimeter of the grey area?

method.method_draft: View the grey region as the part of the middle unit circle left after three neighboring unit circles cut into it, as shown in the image. For each neighboring circle, label its two intersection points with the middle circle. On the grey perimeter, the arc of the middle circle between those two points that would have been part of the original circumference is replaced by the corresponding arc of the neighboring circle. Since the two circles have the same radius and share the same chord, the replaced arc and the added arc have equal length. Therefore each overlap makes no net change to the perimeter compared with the circumference of the middle circle. The grey perimeter is thus equal to the circumference of one radius-1 circle, so it is 2π.
